slides.title: Technical reference directory
keyPoints: Chapter 26
Technical reference directory
Interactive lecture with code, output, and presenter script
slides.narration: Welcome to Book I, Chapter 26: Technical reference directory. This deck is built like the Chapter 1 lecture: the slide gives the conceptual claim, the workbench gives the code or evidence, and presenter notes tell you exactly what to say and do. The goal is not to rush through syntax. The goal is to make every claim accountable to an artifact: source text, compiler behavior, runtime output, an invariant, or a documented design boundary. Start by orienting learners to the chapter, then keep asking the same professional question: what would prove this explanation is true?
actions: Navigate to Book I -> Chapter 26: Technical reference directory -> Slides.
Open Presenter script and directions for yourself; keep the audience on the slide/workbench view.
Tell the audience that code panels are for prediction first, execution second, explanation always.

question.prompt: What makes this a lecture rather than just a reading view?
question.answer: Every slide pairs explanation with a presenter action, a check question, and when possible code or output evidence.

slides.title: What you will be able to explain

slides.narration: By the end of this lecture, learners should be able to explain Technical reference directory without hiding behind recognition. Recognition sounds like, 'I have seen this syntax.' Explanation sounds like, 'Here is the boundary, here is the rule, and here is the output or state that proves the rule held.' This is a graduate-level habit even in an introductory C++ chapter: separate the language form from the engineering evidence. When you teach this, keep moving from vocabulary to mechanism to verification.
actions: Read the targets once without expanding them into a mini lecture.
Ask learners which target is easiest to fake by memorization and which requires evidence.
Use their answer to frame the first concept slide.

question.prompt: What is the difference between recognizing syntax and explaining behavior?
question.answer: Recognizing syntax names a form; explaining behavior connects the form to state, control flow, output, diagnostics, or another observable artifact.

slides.title: Lecture roadmap
keyPoints: ARRAY — Fixed-size array container
CHARCONV — Primitive numeric conversions
CLANG — Clang C++ language support

slides.narration: Here is the path through Chapter 26. The chapter is not a pile of isolated facts; it is a sequence of decisions. First, identify the requirement or contract. Next, choose the language mechanism that fits that contract. Then read or run the example to check the consequence. Finally, use the practice question to decide whether the idea transferred to a new case. As the instructor, keep learners from treating the roadmap as a table of contents. Treat it as a chain of dependencies.
actions: Point to each roadmap item and say what evidence will count later in the deck.
Tell learners that code output will be interpreted line by line, not merely displayed.
Advance only after the class can name the first boundary to watch.

question.prompt: Why teach the roadmap before the syntax?
question.answer: Because learners need to know which problem the syntax is solving; otherwise they memorize form without understanding the contract.

slides.narration: Close Chapter 26 by having learners restate the chapter in one engineering sentence. For Technical reference directory, that sentence should include the mechanism, the boundary, and the evidence. Then ask for the thing most likely to fool a beginner: confusing a printed value with correctness, ignoring stderr, assuming exit status proves output, or trusting a diagram without checking code. The homework move is small but serious: make one controlled change, predict the new output, run it, and write the explanation in terms of source behavior.

slides.title: Check a measured environment report
keyPoints: Return true only if compiler and library are both available and the measured language tag is at least 202002. The function evaluates reported facts; it does not detect installed tools.
slides.narration: A Boolean conjunction directly expresses the three independent requirements. Passing the facts makes boundary tests independent of this machine. Success requires every stated fact, including the language-version boundary. Alternative: An environment probe can gather facts, but mixing detection and evaluation makes controlled unit tests harder.

slides.title: Append only inside a logical size limit
keyPoints: Append value only when it is -100 through 100 and size is below limit. Otherwise return false unchanged. limit is at most 100. Allocation failures may propagate; they are not represented by false.
slides.narration: A size check enforces the user-visible bound before push_back. Capacity stays an implementation storage fact. A false return preserves values and size. Successful append adds exactly one allowed element while staying within limit. Alternative: A fixed std::array is better for a truly fixed extent. Here the logical count varies, so a vector fits the requirement.

slides.title: Keep quotient and remainder consistent
keyPoints: items must be 0 through 1000 and group 1 through 100. Throw std::invalid_argument("range") otherwise. Return complete groups and leftover items.
slides.narration: Integer quotient and remainder express complete groups without introducing floating-point rounding. items equals groups times group plus remainder, and remainder is smaller than group. Alternative: Repeated subtraction can produce the same values but does unnecessary work and adds a loop invariant to maintain.
actions: Predict the output before running.

question.prompt: Which line establishes the promised result?
question.answer: items equals groups times group plus remainder, and remainder is smaller than group.

slides.title: Read one whole bounded count
keyPoints: Accept exactly one integer from 0 through 20, with optional surrounding stream whitespace. Reject empty, malformed, out-of-range, and trailing non-whitespace text. On rejection leave output unchanged.
slides.narration: A temporary separates parsing from committing caller state. A stream matches the whitespace rule and the beginner input lesson. A rejected field preserves the old output; an accepted field consumes the whole permitted field and satisfies 0 through 20. Alternative: from_chars is useful for strict byte-range parsing, but it has different whitespace rules that the adapter must handle explicitly.

slides.title: Increment without signed overflow
keyPoints: Return value plus one when representable as int. At the maximum int throw std::out_of_range("overflow") before arithmetic.
slides.narration: Checking numeric_limits makes the representation boundary explicit before addition. The function returns a value and does not mutate caller state. No path evaluates overflowing signed addition; accepted values increase by exactly one. Alternative: A wider type can help when its range is known to cover the calculation. It still needs a checked conversion to int afterward.

slides.title: Require complete numeric fields
keyPoints: Use from_chars to parse one complete decimal int field, with no whitespace or leading plus. Allow a leading minus only for zero (such as -0); the value must be 0 through 100. Reject an empty or partial field and preserve output on failure.
slides.narration: from_chars exposes conversion status and the stopping position. A temporary protects the prior output from rejected text. Success consumes every byte and produces 0 through 100; failure preserves the previous output. Alternative: Stream extraction supports a different whitespace policy. It still needs complete-field and domain checks to meet this stricter contract.

slides.title: Establish a valid interval at construction
keyPoints: Interval(int low,int high) accepts -100 through 100 endpoints with low<=high. Reject invalid construction with std::invalid_argument("range"). low() const and high() const report the endpoints. A one-point interval is valid.
slides.narration: The initializer list supplies member values, and the constructor rejects a relationship that cannot establish the invariant. No successfully constructed invalid interval escapes. Every live successfully constructed Interval has -100<=low<=high<=100. Alternative: A factory returning an explicit failure value is useful when rejected input is expected control flow. A public unvalidated pair leaves the invariant to every caller.

slides.title: Return a nullable borrowed selection
keyPoints: Return a pointer to the first element greater than threshold, or nullptr if none. Do not change or copy the vector. The pointer borrows its element and must not outlive or survive invalidation of that element.
slides.narration: A pointer expresses both a live borrowed result and absence. The reference loop obtains addresses of actual vector elements rather than temporary copies. A successful result points at the first strictly qualifying live element; nullptr represents no match. Alternative: An optional index can avoid carrying an address across vector edits. It still requires a valid index and an unchanged intended selection meaning.
